subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Infertility is the failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. In East Africa, infections, malnutrition and herbal remedies are common causes. A systematic history, basic exam and affordable tests guide management.

sections.p: Infertility is defined as the inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected sex in a healthy couple. Diagnosis requires a 12‑month history, confirmation of ovulation, and assessment of the partner’s semen.
b: Unexplained infertility – no identifiable cause after work‑up
Primary infertility – never conceived; secondary – failed a previous pregnancy

t.b: Rule out thyroid, prolactin, diabetes – abnormal results suggest endocrine causes
Detect uterine fibroids, ovarian cysts, tubal patency (if available) – normal findings reduce surgical suspicion
Assess volume, concentration, motility, morphology – abnormality indicates male factor infertility

sections.p: Infertility is staged by cause and duration. The WHO classification of male factor infertility grades sperm concentration and motility. Tubal disease is staged by extent of blockage.
b: WHO Grade I – mild male factor; Grade III – severe

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. Other common causes include malnutrition, hormonal imbalance and traditional medicine.
b: Malnutrition – protein‑energy wasting affects ovarian reserve

sections.p: Patients report a long period of trying to conceive with no success. Women may have irregular periods, pain, or history of infections. Men may notice low libido or erectile dysfunction.
b: History of fever or genital ulcers

sections.p: Use the most affordable tests available. When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues and basic labs.
b: Urine pregnancy test – rule out pregnancy before investigations

sections.p: Urgent referral is needed for signs of severe infection, haemorrhage or ectopic pregnancy.
b: Severe genital ulceration – risk of HIV transmission

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then offer assisted reproduction if needed. In low‑resource settings, focus on affordable, evidence‑based care.
b: Refer for IVF only if other options fail and resources allow

sections.p: Regular review every 3–6 months. Prevention focuses on STI control, malaria prophylaxis and safe sexual practices.
b: Counselling on family planning and safe sex

sections.p: Infertility can be mistaken for subfertility, early menopause or contraceptive failure.
b: Contraceptive failure – use of barrier methods with incorrect use

sections.p: Some tests may give false negatives or positives in low‑resource settings.
b: Rapid HIV test – window period may miss recent infection

faq.q: How do you differentiate primary from secondary infertility?
faq.a: Primary infertility is never having conceived; secondary is failure after a previous successful pregnancy.

faq.q: Which infection is most common cause of tubal infertility in East Africa?
faq.a: Chlamydia trachomatis, often asymptomatic, leading to tubal scarring.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with 18 months of infertility and a history of untreated PID presents. What is the next best investigation? — Pelvic ultrasound to assess tubal patency and ovarian reserve.
A 32‑year‑old man has azoospermia on semen analysis. What is the most likely cause in a low‑resource setting? — Undiagnosed HIV or untreated STIs causing testicular damage.
A patient with infertility is taking an herbal abortifacient. What is the most probable mechanism of infertility? — Antagonism of gonadotrophin‑releasing hormone leading to ovarian suppression.
A couple has unexplained infertility after normal work‑up. What is the first assisted reproduction option? — Intrauterine insemination if male factor is mild and facilities exist.
A woman with infertility has a normal FSH but irregular periods. What endocrine disorder should be ruled out? — Hypothyroidism.
A patient presents with infertility and severe anemia. What urgent condition must be excluded? — Ectopic pregnancy or severe infection.
A 25‑year‑old woman with infertility has a history of malaria. What is the likely impact on fertility? — Malaria‑related anemia and possible ovarian dysfunction.
A man with infertility is on a pesticide‑heavy farm. What is a potential cause? — Environmental toxin exposure causing sperm DNA damage.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam identify the most common reversible causes of infertility in low‑resource settings and guide the limited investigations that are available.
b: Duration of unprotected intercourse, regularity of cycles and timing of intercourse; ask about contraception lapses.
Previous pregnancies, miscarriages, stillbirths and outcomes of any assisted reproduction.
History of sexually transmitted infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, genital ulcers or tuberculosis.
Menstrual pattern: length, flow, dysmenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea; ask about galactorrhoea and hot flashes.
Weight loss, malnutrition, chronic illness (malaria, HIV, TB), alcohol, tobacco, pesticide exposure, herbal abortifacients.
Partner history: prior paternity, testicular trauma, varicocele, occupational exposures, prior STI or genital discharge.

t.b: Look for signs of chronic disease (cachexia, pallor, jaundice) and genital skin lesions; positive findings suggest systemic causes or infection.
Palpate for uterine size, adnexal masses or tenderness; a tender uterus may indicate PID, a firm enlarged uterus suggests fibroids.
Assess cervical discharge, ulceration or mucopurulent cervicitis; positive mucopurulent discharge supports PID or STI.
Palpate uterus, ovaries and adnexa; fixed, tender tubes suggest PID, while a cystic mass may be a hydrosalpinx.
Apply gentle pressure on the cervix; pain on movement indicates PID or severe endometriosis.
Palpate left scrotal veins; a palpable, compressible mass that enlarges with Valsalva indicates varicocele, a common male factor.
Assess size, consistency and presence of nodules; small firm testes with high FSH suggest primary testicular failure.
Physical signs cannot quantify sperm count, ovarian reserve or tubal patency; imaging or labs are required for definitive diagnosis.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use the most affordable, locally available tests first; when a test is unavailable, rely on clinical algorithms and basic labs to decide next steps.
b: Urine pregnancy test – rule out pregnancy before any work‑up; a positive result redirects to obstetric care.

t.b: Evaluates ovarian reserve; FSH > 10 IU/L suggests diminished reserve, but normal FSH does not exclude early premature ovarian insufficiency.
Elevated LH > 10 IU/L with high FSH supports ovarian failure; normal LH with high FSH may indicate hypothalamic dysfunction.
Low estradiol < 50 pg/mL with high FSH/LH indicates ovarian failure; high estradiol may mask FSH elevation.
Values > 25 ng/mL suggest hyperprolactinaemia; treat before further fertility work‑up.
TSH > 2.5 mIU/L or < 0.4 mIU/L impairs fertility; aim for 0.5‑2.5 mIU/L before attempting conception.
Progesterone > 30 nmol/L (≈ 9.4 ng/mL) confirms ovulation; lower values suggest anovulation.
Assesses tubal patency; spill of contrast into peritoneal cavity indicates patent tubes; no spill suggests obstruction or severe adhesions.
Evaluates uterine anatomy, ovarian volume and antral follicle count; antral count < 5 suggests low ovarian reserve.
AMH < 1 ng/mL indicates reduced ovarian reserve; useful when FSH is equivocal.

t.a: Serology for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C
t.b: Positive results modify infection‑related management and counselling.

t.a: TB PCR or GeneXpert on endometrial sample
t.b: Detects genital tuberculosis, a common cause of tubal blockage in low‑resource settings.
Use clinical proxies: e.g., regular ovulatory cycles and mid‑luteal progesterone > 30 nmol/L can replace luteal phase testing; palpable varicocele can stand in for Doppler ultrasound.

sections.p: Classification integrates cause, duration and severity to guide management and referral decisions.
b: Primary infertility: never achieved pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse.
Secondary infertility: failure to conceive after a prior pregnancy, same time frame.
Male factor: abnormal semen analysis per WHO criteria; grade severity by sperm concentration (mild ≥ 10 million/mL, moderate 5‑9 million/mL, severe < 5 million/mL).

Female factor – ovulatory: irregular cycles, anovulation confirmed by low progesterone or ultrasound; PCOS diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3: oligo‑/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries).
Female factor – tubal: HSG or laparoscopy shows blockage or adhesions; grade as unilateral or bilateral obstruction.
Female factor – uterine: fibroids, septum, intra‑uterine synechiae; severity based on size/location and impact on cavity.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic infertility must be considered, especially when routine work‑up is normal.

t.a: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) vs. adrenal hyperandrogenism
t.b: Both cause anovulation; measure serum DHEAS and 17‑OH progesterone – elevated DHEAS suggests adrenal source, normal points to PCOS.
Both cause menstrual irregularity; check TSH and prolactin – isolated high prolactin with normal TSH indicates prolactinoma.
Both cause tubal blockage; TB often has systemic symptoms, positive Mantoux/IGRA and endometrial PCR; PID shows acute pelvic pain and cervical discharge.

t.a: Premature ovarian insufficiency vs. normal aging
t.b: Both raise FSH; early age (< 40) with amenorrhoea and low AMH suggests POI, whereas age‑related decline shows gradual FSH rise and preserved AMH.

t.a: Male hypogonadism vs. primary testicular failure
t.b: Both have low testosterone; primary failure shows elevated FSH/LH, whereas hypogonadotropic hypogonadism shows low or normal gonadotropins.

sections.p: A pragmatic ladder for infertility in low‑resource settings, beginning with reversible causes and progressing to assisted reproduction, with clear points for monitoring and referral.
b: 1. Confirm no current pregnancy with urine hCG; counsel couple on timing of intercourse (every 2‑3 days throughout cycle).
2. Treat identifiable infections (e.g., doxycycline + metronidazole for PID, azithromycin for chlamydia) and ensure safe contraception is stopped.
3. Optimize nutrition and correct micronutrient deficiencies (iron, folate, vitamin D) before further work‑up.
4. Perform basic hormonal panel (FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH) and semen analysis; interpret using WHO reference ranges.
5. If ovulatory dysfunction suspected, start letrozole (first‑line for PCOS) or low‑dose clomiphene; avoid clomiphene in thyroid‑uncontrolled patients.
6. For tubal factor, consider hysterosalpingography if available; if not, use hysterosalpingo‑contrast sonography or clinical suspicion to refer for surgical correction.
7. If male factor severe (azoospermia, severe oligozoospermia) and resources allow, discuss ICSI; otherwise, refer for donor sperm or adoption.
8. Escalate to IVF/ICSI only after less invasive measures fail and when financial/logistical support exists; involve multidisciplinary team.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and actions required for the most frequently used agents in infertility treatment.
b: Letrozole – may cause hot flashes, fatigue, mild liver enzyme rise; avoid in pregnancy; monitor liver function if prolonged use.
Clomiphene – risk of visual disturbances, ovarian cysts, multiple pregnancy; stop if >3 cm cyst persists; avoid with uncontrolled thyroid disease.
Metformin (PCOS adjunct) – gastrointestinal upset, rare lactic acidosis; hold before contrast studies; ensure adequate hydration.
Doxycycline – photosensitivity, esophageal irritation; contraindicated in pregnancy; give with food and plenty water.
Azithromycin – QT prolongation risk with other QT‑prolonging drugs; check cardiac history before use.

sections.p: Potential adverse events during evaluation or treatment that mandate urgent referral or higher‑level care.
b: Severe pelvic pain with fever → suspect tubo‑ovarian abscess; arrange urgent imaging and surgical referral.
Sudden abdominal distension, shoulder tip pain → possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy; treat as emergency.
Persistent high FSH (>15 IU/L) with low estradiol → premature ovarian insufficiency; refer for counseling and possible donor gametes.
Azoospermia with normal testicular volume and low testosterone → consider hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; refer for endocrine specialist.

sections.p: Conditions that alter presentation, test interpretation or therapeutic choices in infertility.
b: HIV – may lower sperm quality, increase opportunistic infections; use ART regimens compatible with antiretrovirals; avoid doxycycline in severe neutropenia.
TB genital involvement – causes tubal blockage; obtain GeneXpert or culture; treat with standard anti‑TB regimen before surgery.
Malnutrition – depresses GnRH pulse, lowers AMH; re‑nutrify before hormonal therapy; monitor electrolytes.
Pregnancy – any positive hCG aborts infertility work‑up; repeat test after 2 weeks if doubt.
Diabetes – poor glycaemic control impairs ovulation; optimise HbA1c before ovulation induction.
Herbal abortifacients (e.g., neem, pennyroyal) – may cause uterine toxicity; discontinue and assess endometrial health.
Alcohol excess – reduces testosterone, impairs spermatogenesis; advise abstinence.
Renal or hepatic failure – alter drug clearance (metformin, letrozole); dose‑adjust or avoid.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for populations with unique physiological or socioeconomic needs.
b: Children/adolescents – focus on education, prevention of STIs; defer fertility treatment until reproductive maturity.
Pregnant women – infertility work‑up halted; manage underlying conditions (e.g., thyroid) for current pregnancy.
Elderly (>40 y) – ovarian reserve markedly reduced; prioritize donor oocytes or adoption; counsel on higher miscarriage risk.
People with HIV – ensure viral suppression; use sperm washing for assisted reproduction; avoid drugs that interact with protease inhibitors.
Low‑resource settings – rely on clinical diagnosis (e.g., cervical motion tenderness for PID), use urine hCG, basic semen analysis, and inexpensive ovulation kits; refer only when essential.

facts: Infertility: no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse.
Primary infertility: never conceived; secondary infertility: failure after a previous pregnancy.
Mid‑luteal progesterone >30 nmol/L (≈9.4 ng/mL) confirms ovulation.
TSH target for fertility <2.5 mIU/L; hypothyroidism >2.5 mIU/L, hyperthyroidism <0.4 mIU/L.
Serum FSH >10 IU/L in women >35 y suggests diminished ovarian reserve; normal FSH does NOT exclude premature ovarian insufficiency.
Male primary testicular failure: elevated FSH, low testosterone.
Pelvic inflammatory disease diagnosis: cervical motion tenderness, uterine/adnexal tenderness, and mucopurulent discharge.

vivas.q: Define primary and secondary infertility and give the time frame used for diagnosis.
vivas.a: Primary infertility is never having achieved a pregnancy; secondary infertility is failure to conceive after a prior pregnancy. Diagnosis requires 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse.

vivas.q: What is the first bedside investigation for suspected pelvic inflammatory disease?
vivas.a: Perform a speculum exam looking for mucopurulent cervical discharge and a bimanual exam for cervical motion tenderness; a positive finding suggests PID.

vivas.q: Why is the post‑coital test no longer recommended routinely?
vivas.a: It has poor predictive value, low reproducibility, and does not change management; therefore guidelines have removed it from routine work‑up.

vivas.q: Interpret a mid‑luteal serum progesterone of 8 ng/mL (≈26 nmol/L).
vivas.a: Level is below the ovulation threshold (>30 nmol/L); suggests anovulation and warrants ovulation induction work‑up.

vivas.q: A woman has a normal FSH but irregular periods. Does this rule out premature ovarian insufficiency?
vivas.a: No; early or mild POI can have normal FSH, especially if only menstrual irregularity is present.

vivas.q: What does an elevated serum FSH with azoospermia indicate in a male?
vivas.a: Primary testicular failure (spermatogenic failure) – the testes are not producing sperm, leading to high gonadotropins.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a serum TSH of 3.0 mIU/L in a woman trying to conceive.
vivas.a: TSH >2.5 mIU/L may impair fertility; treatment to lower TSH improves conception rates.

vivas.q: How would you differentiate tubal factor infertility from male factor on basic work‑up?
vivas.a: Normal semen analysis points to tubal factor; hysterosalpingography or laparoscopy then assesses tubal patency.

vivas.q: List three key history questions for infertility assessment.
vivas.a: Duration of trying, frequency of intercourse, timing relative to ovulation; menstrual pattern; prior STIs, PID, surgeries, contraceptive use, and exposure to toxins.

vivas.q: Describe how to perform a basic bimanual pelvic exam and what a positive cervical motion tenderness indicates.
vivas.a: Insert two fingers into the vagina, palpate uterus and adnexa; gently move the cervix. Pain on movement indicates PID or endometriosis.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line ovulation induction drug for PCOS and why?
vivas.a: Letrozole; it lowers estrogen feedback, increases FSH, has higher live‑birth rates and lower multiple‑pregnancy risk than clomiphene.

vivas.q: When is IVF indicated in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: After thorough evaluation and failure of less invasive treatments, when tubal factor is irreversible or male factor is severe and resources allow.

vivas.q: A 28‑year‑old woman with untreated PID presents after 18 months of trying. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Obtain semen analysis, confirm ovulation (mid‑luteal progesterone), and assess tubal patency with hysterosalpingography.

vivas.q: A 32‑year‑old man has azoospermia on semen analysis. What is the most likely cause in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Obstructive cause such as untreated epididymal infection or prior surgery; evaluate with scrotal ultrasound if available.

vivas.q: A patient taking an herbal abortifacient presents with infertility. What mechanism most likely explains the effect?
vivas.a: Phytoestrogens or alkaloids can disrupt the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑ovarian axis, leading to anovulation.

vivas.q: What is the first assisted reproduction technique for unexplained infertility after normal work‑up?
vivas.a: Intra‑uterine insemination (IUI) with controlled ovarian stimulation.

vivas.q: A woman with normal FSH but irregular periods likely has which endocrine disorder?
vivas.a: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) – insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism can cause irregular cycles despite normal FSH.

vivas.q: What urgent condition must be excluded in a patient with infertility and severe anemia?
vivas.a: Ectopic pregnancy, which can cause bleeding and anemia; obtain quantitative β‑hCG and transvaginal ultrasound.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with a 14‑day menstrual cycle has a serum progesterone of 10 ng/mL on day 21. Which statement is correct?
o: Progesterone is too low for luteal phase

mcqs.q: A man with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with infertility. Which hormone pattern is expected?
mcqs.e: Primary testicular failure gives elevated FSH/LH and low testosterone.

mcqs.q: Which thyroid TSH range is optimal for a woman trying to conceive?
mcqs.e: Guidelines aim for TSH <2.5 mIU/L in fertility patients.

mcqs.q: A 25‑year‑old woman with infertility has a history of malaria. Which reproductive effect is most likely?
o: Reduced ovarian reserve due to malaria‑induced inflammation
mcqs.e: Severe malaria can impair ovarian function and reduce reserve.

cases.v: 28‑year‑old woman, 18 months trying, history of untreated PID, regular cycles, BMI 22, no contraception.

qs.q: What three investigations should you order first?
qs.a: Semen analysis of partner, mid‑luteal progesterone, and hysterosalpingography to assess tubal patency.

qs.q: If hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal blockage, what is the next management step?
qs.a: Discuss assisted reproduction; intra‑uterine insemination is ineffective, so refer for IVF if resources allow.

qs.q: Which bedside sign would support ongoing PID and how is it elicited?
qs.a: Cervical motion tenderness: gentle movement of the cervix during bimanual exam causing pain indicates PID.

cases.v: 32‑year‑old man, azoospermia on semen analysis, history of pesticide exposure, small firm testes, elevated FSH, low testosterone.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Primary testicular failure (Klinefelter‑like or toxic orchitis) causing azoospermia.

qs.q: Which additional test helps differentiate obstructive from non‑obstructive azoospermia?
qs.a: Scrotal ultrasound to assess epididymal and testicular architecture; absence of dilated ducts suggests non‑obstructive.

qs.q: What fertility option is realistic in this setting?
qs.a: If sperm retrieval is possible, consider ICSI; otherwise discuss donor sperm or adoption.

mistakes: Assuming normal FSH excludes premature ovarian insufficiency – early POI can have normal FSH.
Using the post‑coital test routinely – it is no longer recommended due to low predictive value.
Treating PID with doxycycline alone without covering chlamydia and gonorrhoea or noting pregnancy contraindication.
Confusing the progesterone thresholds (mixing ng/mL and nmol/L) – use consistent conversion.
Interpreting elevated FSH in men as normal testosterone – primary testicular failure usually has low testosterone.
Ordering hysterosalpingography without first confirming ovulation – ovulation must be proven before tubal assessment.
Neglecting to screen for HIV or TB, which can alter fertility and affect treatment choices.
Prescribing clomiphene as first‑line for PCOS without considering letrozole, which has better outcomes.
